sub_unit_name: Corrosion: Causes and effects of corrosion - Theories of chemical and electrochemical corrosion - Mechanism of electrochemical corrosion

content.title: Corrosion
content.description: Corrosion is the gradual deterioration of a metal due to chemical or electrochemical reactions with its surrounding environment. It leads to loss of metal, reduced strength, and economic loss.

content.content: Corrosion is a major problem in engineering industries as it damages machines, pipelines, bridges, ships, and buildings. The two main theories explaining corrosion are chemical corrosion and electrochemical corrosion.

content.title: Effects of Corrosion
content.content: Corrosion causes loss of metal, decreases mechanical strength, increases maintenance costs, and may lead to equipment failure.

items.question: Moisture and Oxygen
items.answer: Water and oxygen accelerate corrosion of metals.

items.question: Acids and Salts
items.answer: Acidic and saline environments increase corrosion rate.

items.question: Impurities
items.answer: Impurities in metals create corrosion cells.

content.content: Chemical (Dry) corrosion occurs when a metal reacts directly with dry gases such as oxygen, sulfur, or chlorine without the presence of moisture. It usually occurs at high temperatures and forms an oxide layer on the metal surface.

Electrochemical (Wet) corrosion occurs in the presence of moisture or an electrolyte. Tiny anodic and cathodic regions are formed on the metal surface. Oxidation occurs at the anode, while reduction occurs at the cathode, resulting in gradual metal loss.

content.title: Industrial Importance
content.content: Understanding corrosion helps engineers select suitable materials and protective methods, increasing the life of engineering structures.

content.title: Quick Revision
points: Corrosion is the deterioration of metals.
Chemical corrosion occurs in dry environments.
Electrochemical corrosion occurs in the presence of moisture.
Rusting of iron is a common example of electrochemical corrosion.
